title: Leading On Our Worst Day
author: Honest Office
summary: Argues that the goal of leadership development is not creating flawless leaders, but building self-awareness of natural gifts and limitations so leaders can recognize when they're off course. Introduces the concept of 'Leadership Grinches'—negative patterns that emerge particularly on worst days when fatigue and stress cause leaders to revert to unhelpful behaviors. Identifies five common manifestations: the Micromanager (hovering, killing initiative), the Gatekeeper (hoarding information and decision authority), the Untouchable (operating without accountability), the All-Knowing (dismissing ideas due to title/tenure), and the Comforter (avoiding hard conversations for ease). The piece emphasizes that leaders don't need to be perfect or avoid bad days, but need self-awareness, the ability to pause and adjust course, repair trust, and actively work to keep their Leadership Grinches in check. When leaders understand their blind spots and adjust accordingly, teams spend less time managing the leader and more time doing actual work.
points: Leadership development is about understanding natural gifts and limitations, not achieving flawlessness; self-awareness enables leaders to recognize when they're off course before damage escalates.
The five Leadership Grinches—Micromanager, Gatekeeper, Untouchable, All-Knowing, Comforter—manifest most dangerously on worst days when stress and fatigue lower self-regulation.
The Micromanager kills initiative by hovering, the Gatekeeper blocks collaboration through information hoarding, and the All-Knowing shuts down feedback and learning through false certainty.
The Untouchable's lack of accountability and the Comforter's conflict avoidance both erode team trust and undermine progress in different ways but with similar impact.
The power of self-awareness lies in enabling leaders to pause, adjust course, repair relationships, and return to their best selves rather than pretending perfection or hiding poor behavior.
quotes: My goal in developing people has never been about getting us to a place where we're flawless, cheery, Who-like creatures who deliver a perfectly curated A-game every single moment.
No one leads at their best all the time, and as human beings, we'd be ignorant to expect such a thing.

Sometimes they surface as the Micromanager, hovering ever so closely that your team starts to wonder what they're doing there while slowly internalizing the idea that it's safer to wait for direction than take initiative.
The All-Knowing is another Leadership Grinch, which often looks like the dismissal of ideas because they're convinced they already have the answer given their title or tenure.
There's considerable power in self-awareness—in knowing how and when our Leadership Grinches might surface. When we do, people spend less time managing us and more time doing the work.

What we need are leaders who understand their blind spots, and who have the awareness to pause, adjust, repair, and find a way back to the best parts of their leadership.” Archived from Honest Office Substack on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
